title: Chapter 44: Sterling's Gift, Part 3 of 5: First Light
html:
The doctor had a barrow.
It was the barrow he used for the dead. Lyra knew that without being told. A long flat handcart of gray wood, with two high iron-shod wheels and two long handles, and a canvas cover that tied down at the corners. There was a smell in the wood that no amount of scrubbing would ever take out. Not a bad smell. Lime, and vinegar, and something under them that was sweet and old, like a cupboard where apples have been kept too long.
They laid Corin in it at the fifth bell.
Oren lifted him. Silas held the leg. They put him down on a bed of sacks in the bottom of the barrow, on his back, with the stiff leg out straight and a rolled blanket under the heel so the wheels would not jar it, and the Ledger inside his coat against his chest, buttoned in. He woke for a moment while they did it. He looked up at the curved brick roof of the arch, and then at Lyra's face over him, and said, quite clearly, "Don't let them put the lid on."
"We won't," said Lyra.
He shut his eyes again.
They did not put the lid on. Silas spread a gray blanket over him, up to the chin, and then a sheet of oiled canvas over that, against the snow, and left his face bare. Then the doctor took a small square of white card out of his own coat pocket, and a stub of pencil, and wrote on it in big black letters, and tied it to the end of the barrow with a piece of string, where anybody coming up behind would see it.
FEVER. KEEP BACK. BY ORDER OF THE PARISH DOCTOR, ST BRIDE'S.
"There," he said. "That's better than a warrant. A constable will stop a warrant. He won't stop a fever." He looked at Lyra. "Pull your cap down. You're my boy, carrying the bag. You don't talk. If anybody talks to you, cough."
Lyra pulled the cap down.
She had worn it for three days now. Ellis's cap, the flat gray one, too big for her, that came down over her ears and hid the place where her hair had been cut off short with the doctor's knife. She had Silas's black bag in one hand, and it was heavy, and it clinked. In the other hand she had nothing. She kept wanting to put it on the Ledger, inside her coat. But the Ledger was not there. It was in the barrow, buttoned into Corin's coat, where it belonged.
Gideon came out of the shadows by the second brazier with his sling and his new brown boots and stood beside her.
"I'm your other boy," he said to the doctor. "I push."
"You've got one arm."
"I've got one arm that works," said Gideon. "And two legs. And no big toes. I can push."
Silas looked at him for a moment. Then he nodded.
Bet came last. She had her bundle, and a shawl of Mother Grue's tied round her head and crossed over her chest and knotted at the back, the way the women of the Lower Docks tied them, so that only her round red face showed in the middle, like a moon in a cloud. She went and stood at the end of the barrow by the doctor's card, and put her hand on the gray wood.
Oren lifted the handles.
Mother Grue stood at the mouth of the arch, with the canvas held back in one hand, and watched them go. She was going last. She and Abel's wife and the three old women from the second arch, by the river path, at the half bell. She did not say goodbye. She looked at Corin's gray face in the barrow as it went past her, and at the white card on its string, and at Lyra.
"Mind the Steps," she said. "They're glass, this morning."
They were.
The Steps went up from the river to the street in a long crooked flight of old stone, worn into hollows in the middle by a hundred years of feet, and every hollow was full of ice. Black ice, hard and smooth, with a skin of new snow on top of it so that you could not see it until your boot went out from under you. Oren took the barrow up them backward. One step at a time. Leaning his whole weight back against the handles, with his heels dug in, and the iron wheels banging up from step to step behind him, bang, and a stop, and bang. Gideon pushed from below with his one good hand and his shoulder. Silas walked beside the barrow holding the edge of the canvas, saying steady, steady, very low. Lyra walked behind with the bag, and Bet beside her, holding her coat.
Forty-two steps. Lyra counted them.
At the top, Oren set the barrow down on the flat, and stood with his head down and his big hands on his knees, breathing. Steam came off him in the cold like smoke off a horse.
The sky was beginning to go gray.
Not light. Not yet. But the black had gone thin over the roofs on the far side of the river, and you could see the shapes of the chimneys against it, and the long line of the bridge, and the snow coming down out of it, slow and soft, gray on gray. The street at the top of the Steps was empty. A long street of tall narrow warehouses with their doors shut and their windows dark, and a lamp at the corner that had burned out in the night and stood there with snow on its glass hat, and nothing else at all.
Lyra turned and looked back down.
You could see the arches from here. The whole long row of them, along the bottom of the river wall, eleven black mouths in the brick, like the gills of a fish. The canvas over the mouth of the first one. The thin line of smoke still going up from the brazier inside, gray in the gray light. And the river below it, wide and slow and white with ice at the edges, grinding.
And along the river path, from the east, from the bridges, lanterns.
Six of them. Moving. Swinging. In a line.
Lyra did not move.
"Girl," said Silas, very low.
She did not move.
The lanterns came along the river path at a walk. Not hurrying. Six men, in long coats, with their collars up, and something on their shoulders that caught the lantern light in a long dull gleam. Hooks. The long iron hooks of the Inquisition, that they used for dragging canals. And in front of them, a seventh man, without a lantern, in a round hat and a dark coat, walking with his hands behind his back. Not fast. Pleasantly. The way a man walks down a street on a Sunday to look at the houses.
Gant.
She could not see his face. She did not need to. She had seen it before, close, and it had seen her. And it was in the Ledger, where Corin had written it down. Round pink cheeks. A pleasant smile.
The lanterns came to the first arch, and stopped.
Gant stood in front of the canvas. He did not touch it. He said something, and one of the men stepped forward and lifted the canvas back on the end of his hook, and held it up, and the light of six lanterns went in under the black brick.
Nothing happened.
Then the men went in. One at a time, stooping. The lanterns went in after them, and the light moved along inside the arch, and came out a little way along, through the gaps where the arches joined, a yellow glow moving from one black mouth to the next. Second arch. Third.
Lyra heard the sound.
Thin. High. Very far away, down there by the river, under the brick, and the grinding of the ice. Like a kettle. Like a dog shut out in the snow.
It went on and on.
"Girl," said Silas again. And this time he put his hand on her arm.
She did not shake it off. She stood at the top of the Steps with the doctor's bag in one hand and his long thin fingers on her arm, and watched.
The sound stopped. All at once. Like a door shutting.
Then two of the lanterns came out of the mouth of the third arch. And between them, a thin dark shape that hung between two men with its feet dragging, the way Corin had hung between Gideon and Remy at the bottom of the Steps a few hours ago. Except that Corin had been trying to walk. This one was not. It hung, and its head hung, and its arms hung, and the two men carried it along the river path like a sack, toward the bridge, toward the lanterns that were waiting there.
Gant came out after them. He stood at the mouth of the third arch with his hands behind his back and watched them go.
Then he turned his head.
Not fast. Pleasantly. And looked up.
Up the river wall. Up the long crooked flight of the Steps. Up to the top, where the gray light was coming, and the snow was falling, and a doctor stood beside his barrow with his boy and his bag.
Lyra felt it. Like a cold hand laid flat on the middle of her back.
She did not move. She could not. She stood very still with her cap down over her ears and her face in its shadow, and Gant looked up at her, and she looked down at him, across the whole width of the gray morning, two hundred yards, more, through the falling snow.
Then Bet coughed.
A long, dry, hacking cough, that bent her double, there by the end of the barrow, in her shawl, with her hand on the white card that said FEVER.
Gant looked at her for a moment longer.
Then he turned away, and went back into the arch.
"Now," said Silas. "Now. Walk. Don't run."
Oren lifted the handles.
They walked.
Lyra did not look back again. Not at the corner. Not at the next corner, or the one after that, where the long street of warehouses met the bottom of Saint Bride's Hill and began to climb. She walked behind the barrow with the doctor's bag, and Bet beside her, holding her coat. And after a while she said, very low, without turning her head:
"Bet. Was that on purpose?"
Bet did not answer for a moment. Her round red face in its shawl was looking straight ahead, at the end of the barrow, at Corin's boot sticking up under the canvas.
"Ned coughed like that," she said. "At the end. Everyone got out of his way."
She did not say anything else. And Lyra did not ask her anything else. They walked on up the hill in the gray snow, behind the doctor's barrow, and the city woke up round them, shutter by shutter, chimney by chimney, and nobody stopped them at all.
Saint Bride's
Saint Bride's stood at the top of its hill like an old woman who has climbed a long way and sat down to get her breath and never got up again.
It was a small church, and very old. Older than the Bank. Older than the Hill, the doctor said, though Lyra did not see how a church could be older than the hill it stood on. Its stone was black. Not painted black. Black with age and smoke, the way the inside of a chimney is black, so that the snow lying on its ledges and along the tops of its walls looked whiter than snow had any right to look. It had a short square tower with a bell in it, and a clock on the tower that had stopped at twenty past four a long time ago, and nobody had ever started it again. It had narrow windows of plain glass, small greenish panes in lead, and most of them were cracked. It had a porch with a stone bench on each side, worn into hollows by a few hundred years of people sitting down on them to wait.
All round it was the graveyard.
The graves went down the hill on every side, in crooked rows, between black yew trees that the snow had bent down nearly to the ground. Old stones, leaning. Older stones, fallen flat and grown over with moss and lichen and now with snow, so that they were only long white humps in the white, like sleeping animals. Here and there a new stone, pale and straight and sharp at the corners, with a name on it that you could still read. And at the bottom of the slope, by the iron railings, a long low row of small mounds with no stones at all. Only wooden crosses. Only sticks, some of them, two sticks tied together with string.
Lyra did not count them.
The doctor did not take them in at the porch. He took them round the side, on a path between the graves where the snow had been trodden down into gray slush by a great many feet, to a low door in the wall of the church below the level of the windows. A door half sunk in the ground, with three stone steps going down to it, and a lamp hanging over it on an iron hook, lit, in the daylight.
"Mind the steps," said Silas. "And the smell."
The smell came up the steps to meet them.
It was the same smell that was in the gray wood of the barrow. Lime, and vinegar, and something sweet under them. But here it was stronger. Much stronger. It was not a bad smell, not the smell of rot, nothing like that. It was the smell of pears. Ripe pears, the soft brown kind that have gone past ripe on the windowsill and begun to go to sugar. It filled the air at the bottom of the steps like a warm fog, and Lyra breathed it in, and something in the back of her throat closed up.
Sweet breath, the doctor had said on Monday. Pear breath. That's how you know.
Oren carried Corin down the three steps sideways, with the stiff leg out in front of him, and the doctor held the door.
The crypt of Saint Bride's ran under the whole of the church. Lyra had not known that a crypt could be so big. It went away from the door in a long low hall of stone, with a roof that came down in curves onto short thick pillars, row after row of them, like the inside of a great stone loaf. Each pillar had a lamp on it, on an iron bracket. Each lamp made a small round pool of yellow light on the stone floor, and between the pools it was dim and brown and warm. Warmer than the arches. Much warmer. There were braziers burning all down the middle of the hall, six of them, and someone had hung blankets over the far door to keep the heat in.
And between the pillars, in the pools of light, the beds.
They were not proper beds. They were straw mattresses on boards, on bricks, on old church pews that had been taken up from somewhere and laid end to end. And on each one, a child. Some of them sitting up. Some of them lying down with their faces to the wall. Some of them asleep, with their mouths open and their breath going in and out, slow and sweet.
Fifty-two, the doctor had said. That had been on Sunday. Before Ned.
Lyra stood just inside the door with the doctor's bag in her hand and looked at them.
None of them looked at her.
That was the first thing she noticed. A crypt full of children, and a stranger in the door, and none of them looked round. Children always looked. Children could not help looking. At Crown Walk, when a visitor came into the nursery, she and Rowan had both looked up at once, every time, like two birds on a branch. These children did not. They sat on their pallets and looked at their hands, or at the wall, or at nothing. A boy of about nine was sitting cross-legged on a pew with a wooden spoon in his hand, turning it over and over, slowly, as if he could not remember what it was for. A girl younger than Bet was lying on her side with her eyes open, looking at the lamp on the pillar beside her, not blinking.
"They're better," said Silas, at her side. Very low. "You wouldn't think so. But they are. Since Monday. Since Nell took the glasses off." He nodded at the girl watching the lamp. "That one couldn't open her eyes on Sunday. Now she can. In a week she might look at you. In a month she might say your name." He paused. "If nobody puts a glass back on her."
"And if somebody does?"
Silas did not answer.
There were women among the beds. Lyra saw them now. Three of them, in gray aprons, moving slowly between the pillars with jugs and cups and cloths. Widows of the parish, the doctor said. They came by the day for a shilling and their dinner. One of them was very old and very small and walked bent nearly double. One of them was young, with a baby tied to her back in a shawl. One of them was large and red and cheerful, and talked to the children all the time in a loud kind voice, whether they answered or not. There's my lamb. There's my good boy. Drink this for Mrs. Doyle, now.
They put Corin in a side vault.
There were several of them, opening off the main hall through low round arches, like chapels. Small rooms of stone, with stone benches round the walls. The one the doctor chose was at the far end, near the blanketed door, where it was warmest. There was a niche in its back wall, and in the niche, behind an iron grille, rows of brown round things stacked one on another, very neatly, like loaves on a baker's shelf.
Lyra looked at them for a moment before she understood they were skulls.
"Old monks," said Silas. "Five hundred years old, some of them. They won't mind." He spread a blanket on the stone bench under the niche. "It's the only room with a bench long enough for that leg."
Oren laid Corin down on the bench, with the stiff leg out along it and his head on a folded sack and the skulls of the old monks looking down at him from behind their grille. Corin did not wake. His face was gray. His breath was slow. Lyra bent over him, close, without meaning to, and breathed in.
No pears. Only lamp oil and soot and the brown medicine.
She straightened up.
In the next vault, on two trestles, there was a box. A plain box of new pale wood, the size of a boy of seven, with the lid nailed down. Somebody had put a sprig of yew on the lid, dark green, and it had dropped some of its needles onto the wood.
Bet went and stood beside it.
She stood there in her shawl with her bundle in her arms, looking at the box, the way Wick had looked at his scraps of paper. Then she put the bundle down on the floor, and untied it, and took something out. A small tin soldier, red and gold, with the paint worn off his face. She put it on the lid of the box, beside the yew. Very carefully. Standing up. And looked at it.
Then she picked up her bundle again and came back and sat down on the floor by the bench where Corin lay, with her back to the wall, and shut her eyes.
Lyra did not say anything to her. She did not know anything to say.
She went back out into the main hall, and found the large red cheerful woman, Mrs. Doyle, and asked her where the water was, and the cloths. And Mrs. Doyle looked at her, at the cap and the cropped hair and the coat that was too big, and at her face, and her hands, which were not the hands of a doctor's boy whatever they had become in two weeks.
And said, quite kindly, "Over there, my lamb. By the far brazier. And mind your sleeves in the hot water, my lady. You'll scald yourself."
Lyra stopped.
Mrs. Doyle had already turned away. She was bending over a pallet, holding a cup to a boy's mouth, talking in her loud kind voice. There's my good boy. Just a sip. Just one more, for Mrs. Doyle.
Lyra stood in the warm brown light with the smell of pears all round her.
Then she went and got the water.
Word from Velvet Street
The word came at the second bell after noon, in a basket of bread.
Lyra had been working all morning. She had carried water, and emptied pails, and held cups to mouths that did not open, and wiped faces that did not know they were being wiped. She had helped the old bent widow, Mrs. Fitch, change the straw on six mattresses, and had learned that you rolled the child gently to one side, like a sleeping dog, and pulled the old straw out from under, and pushed the new straw in, and rolled them back. She had learned that the children did not cry when you did this. That was the worst of it. At Crown Walk, if you had rolled Rowan over in his sleep he would have kicked you.
She had sat with Corin for a while. He had woken at the eleventh bell, and lain on his bench under the skulls of the old monks and looked up at them for a long time without saying anything, and then said, "Well. That's new." And then he had opened the Ledger and read the first page, the way he always did when he woke somewhere strange. Your name is Corin Vane. She had watched his lips move. Then he had looked at her, and known her, and his mouth had gone down at the left corner, and she had gone back to work so that he would not see her face.
Now she was sitting on the floor by the far brazier, with her back to a pillar and a cup of the widows' tea in her hands, black and stewed and very sweet, when the low door at the end of the crypt opened, and let in a slab of white daylight and a gust of snow and a woman with a basket.
She was a big woman, broad as a door, in a brown shawl and a man's boots. Her face was red with cold, and she had a wide flat nose and small bright eyes like a pig's, very clever. Lyra knew her. Not her name. Her kind. She had seen women like her on every set of river steps in the Lower Docks, in the mornings, scrubbing. The step women. They scrubbed the front steps of the great houses on the Hill and the counting houses on the quays and the Watch houses and the churches, every morning, on their knees, with a bucket and a brush, before anybody important was awake. And they saw everything. And they talked to each other. Corin said that the step women of the city knew more than the Inquisition and the Bank put together, and that nobody had ever thought to ask them.
The big woman put the basket down by the door and pulled the cloth off it. Bread. A dozen round brown loaves, still warm, steaming in the cold air from the door.
"From the Hobbses' bakehouse," she said, to Mrs. Doyle. "For the doctor's lambs. Hobbs says there's more tomorrow if the Health don't come sniffing." Then she looked round the crypt, slowly, with her small bright eyes, from pillar to pillar, the way a cat looks round a room.
And her eyes stopped on Lyra.
She came down the hall between the beds. She did not hurry. She stopped in front of Lyra and looked down at her, at the cap and the coat and the cup of tea.
"You're the gray one," she said. Not a question.
Lyra put down the cup.
"Bridie Kane," said the woman. "I do the Bourse kitchen door, mornings, and the Needle and Thimble on Velvet Street, back step, Wednesdays. It was me got your catalogue." She bent down, with a grunt, close, so that nobody else would hear, and her breath smelled of onions and bread. "Madame Hesper says to tell the young lady in gray that there's a parcel come for her. Come yesterday morning. To the shop. By hand. She's been waiting for my Wednesday to send word, since she'd trust nobody else with it."
Lyra did not move.
"By whose hand?"
"Footman." Bridie Kane's small eyes did not leave her face. "Gray livery. Silver buttons. Very tall, very polite, gloves on. Rang at the front, if you please, not the back. Gave it to the girl in the shop and said, For the Lady Lyra Thorne. To be called for. And went off down Velvet Street in the snow like he had all day." She paused. "Madame Hesper says she's not opened it. Madame Hesper says she'd rather not have it in the shop another night. Madame Hesper says she'd like you to come and take it away this afternoon. By the back. Before the fifth bell."
"Gray livery," said Lyra slowly. "Silver buttons."
"That's what I said."
"Whose livery is that?"
Bridie Kane looked at her for a long moment. Then she straightened up, with another grunt, and wiped her hands on her shawl.
"I do the Bank steps, too," she said. "Mondays and Thursdays. Front and side. Gray and silver is the Bank, love. The inside servants. The ones that work upstairs."
She went away down the hall between the beds, and picked up her empty basket, and went out into the snow.
Lyra sat by the pillar for a long time with the cup of tea going cold in her hands.
Then she got up and went to the side vault.
Corin was awake. He was lying on his bench with the Ledger on his chest and his eyes on the skulls in their niche. Gideon was sitting on the floor beside him with his back to the wall, carving something out of a bit of wood with a little knife he held in his good hand, the sling arm in his lap. Bet was asleep, curled up by the bench, with her head on her bundle. Oren was standing in the arch of the vault with his arms folded, the way he had stood all morning, facing the hall.
Lyra told them.
When she had finished, nobody said anything.
Then Corin said, "No."
"I haven't asked you anything."
"You're going to." He did not look away from the skulls. "You're going to say you have to go and get it. And I'm saying no."
"It's my name on it."
"That's why." He turned his head on the folded sack and looked at her. His face was still the lamp boy's face, the broken nose and the white wild eyebrows and the soot, but the paint was beginning to go at the edges now, and under it, in places, his own skin showed through, gray and tired. "Think, Lyra. Somebody at the Bank knows your name. Your real name. Your title. They know you go to Hesper's. They know it well enough to send a parcel there, by the front door, in daylight, with a footman in livery, and walk away." His hand moved on the Ledger. "Who told them?"
"I don't know."
"Neither do I. That's why no."
"If they wanted to catch me," said Lyra, "they wouldn't send a parcel. They'd send Gant." She heard her voice go hard and did not stop it. "They'd have sent six men with hooks to Hesper's on Saturday, when I was there in my mother's gown. They didn't. They sent a footman with a box. Polite. By the front door. To be called for." She folded her arms. "That's not a trap. That's a letter."
"A letter from who?"
"That's what I want to know."
Corin looked at her for a long time.
Then he looked past her, at Oren in the arch.
Oren did not say anything. He did not need to. He unfolded his arms and took Terrence's coat down from the iron hook in the wall where he had hung it to dry, and put it on, and buttoned it to the throat.
"He goes with you," said Corin. "All the way. To the door, and in, and out."
"Yes."
"And you come back by the fifth bell. Not after. If you're not back by the fifth bell—"
"Then you'll lie on that bench under those skulls and worry," said Lyra, "because there's nothing else you can do." She stopped. She had not meant it to come out like that. She saw it go into him. She saw it land on the stiff leg in its splints.
She uncrossed her arms.
"I'm sorry," she said. "That was cruel."
"It was true." His mouth went down at the left corner. "Go on. Before the light goes."
Gideon looked up from his carving.
"Go by Comb Street," he said. "Not the Crescent. The Crescent's got Inquisition on every lamp today. Ask anybody." He went back to his carving. "And don't buy anything."
"Why not?"
"Because you look like a boy who's got money," said Gideon, without looking up, "and that's the only thing in this city worse than looking like a girl who hasn't."
